title: MB7-22430
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, as well as her two minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of the United States, are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which rejected their refugee protection claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, as well as her two minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of the United States, are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which rejected their refugee protection claim.
They are not submitting any new evidence on appeal. They are also not requesting that a hearing be held before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).
The principal appellant, XXXX XXXX, was appointed the designated representative of her two minor children.
In rendering its decision, the RAD considered the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.

Under subsection 111(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA or "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.
In her Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the principal appellant alleges that on XXXX XXXX, 2004, her father, an opponent of President Aristide's government, was shot to death.

The appellant alleges that that same day, she and her sister were sexually assaulted by supporters of President Aristide at the home of their father's friend, a man by the name of XXXX XXXX, where they had been invited.
The appellant left Haiti for the Dominican Republic, to then go to the United States in XXXX 2004, where she applied for asylum, which she was refused.
The appellant alleges that she returned to Haiti on XXXX XXXX, 2017, to be married, and that she and the passengers of the bus on which she was travelling with her husband were robbed.
The appellant returned to the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2017, after getting married. She then went to Canada with her two children to claim refugee protection here.
The minor appellants base their claim on that of their mother.

The RPD rejected the refugee protection claims, first by determining that the evidence submitted established no fear of returning to the United States for the two minor appellants, and then by determining that the evidence submitted did not demonstrate that the principal appellant had a well-founded fear of persecution following the assault in 2004, as she had never had any news of XXXX XXXX and his associates since that incident, and because the robbery in 2017 was an isolated incident.

Before the RAD, the appellants submit that the RPD erred in the following respects: * It failed to consider Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution; * It failed to consider the documentary evidence on sexual violence in Haiti and to analyze the situation of women in that country; * It did not give her sufficient time to find a new lawyer after hers failed to appear on the first hearing date.
For these reasons, the appellants are asking the RAD to set aside the RPD's determination and grant them refugee protection, or alternatively, to refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination.

The role of the RAD is to review RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard of review after conducting its own analysis of the record with a view to determining whether, as the appellant submits, the RPD erred. The exception to this rule concerns the RPD's findings in the assessment of the credibility or weight to be granted to the oral evidence given before it, in situations where it enjoys a particular advantage. The RAD must then apply the standard of reasonableness (Canada v. Huruglica, F.C.A., A-470-14). The reasons will be provided in my analysis if I find that the RPD had a particular advantage. ANALYSIS A. Did the RPD err by failing to consider Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution?
paragraphs.heading_before: STANDARD OF REVIEW AND RAD'S ROLE

paragraphs.text: In my opinion, the answer to this question is no, for the following reasons.
In their memorandum, the appellants do not indicate how the RPD allegedly failed to consider Guideline 4.
Although it is true that the RPD does not explicitly mention in its reasons to have considered it, this does not automatically mean that it did not do so.
I do not see which principles set out in this guideline the RPD apparently failed to consider or apply.

Therefore, the RPD considered in its analysis the fact that the principal appellant had been the victim of a sexual assault, but concluded that she did not have, on the date of the decision, a well-founded fear of persecution on this ground should she return to Haiti. Furthermore, the RPD took into account the fact that the appellant testified that she had wanted to return to Haiti with her husband in 2017, which demonstrated a lack of subjective fear on her part.

In addition, the hearing before the RPD took place in a calm and respectful manner, and the RPD, without ever asking any details on the sexual assault, demonstrated sensitivity by granting the appellant breaks when the matter was addressed and when she testified with great emotion. B. Did the RPD err by failing to consider the documentary evidence on sexual violence in Haiti and to analyze the situation of women in that country?
I find that the answer to this question is no, for the following reasons.

The appellants submit in paragraph 15 of their memorandum that the principal appellant is still traumatized by the sexual assault, and in paragraph 16 that the failure to examine the documentary evidence on sexual violence in Haiti is an error. I am not sure that I understand the link between these two submissions, and I find that the memorandum, except for citing quotes from certain documents in the National Documentation Package, does not contain any detailed submission on the content of these documents or how they apply to the principal appellant's situation.

Regardless, before the RPD, the principal appellant never mentioned a fear of persecution for the sole reason of her gender if she had to return to Haiti. When questioned by the RPD on the reasons why she was claiming refugee protection, the appellant answered by describing the event that had taken place in XXXX 2017, when she and her husband had been robbed and manhandled by thieves. She later added that she feared violence against her and her children in Haiti following this incident in 2017.

Not having alleged any subjective fear by reason of her gender, or by the sole fact that she is a woman, if she had to return to Haiti, the RPD therefore did not err by not conducting an analysis of the documentary evidence regarding the situation of women in that country. C. Did the RPD err by not giving her sufficient time to find a new lawyer after hers failed to appear on the first hearing date?
Once again, I find that the answer to this question is no, for the following reasons.

The appellants appeared for the first time before the RPD on October 11, 2017. The counsel who was to represent them did not appear, and the RPD, through Board personnel, contacted the counsel three times that day. Each time he stated that he would be there in about 15 minutes, but he never appeared.

The RPD then postponed the appellants' hearing until a later date, that is, October 26, 2017, advising the principal appellant to contact her counsel, or to find another if necessary, to proceed on that date.

On October 26, the principal appellant went before the RPD without counsel, explaining that she had twice called the person who was to represent her, but was unable to speak to him and that she was unable to find another counsel available, and that as a result, she wanted to proceed without counsel before the RPD.
At no time did the principal appellant object to proceeding before the RPD without the presence of her counsel. Nor did she ask the RPD to again postpone the hearing so that she could find counsel.

I find that the appellant had an obligation to point out to the RPD her objections to proceeding without being represented by counsel, if she had any, and that this objection cannot later be raised before the RAD following an unfavourable RPD decision.

I add that no evidence was submitted to the RAD of a complaint for professional misconduct submitted to the Barreau du Québec by the appellants against the counsel who was to represent them before the RPD.
In their memorandum, the appellants are not contesting the RPD's decision regarding the minor appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, who are citizens of the United States.

After analyzing all the evidence submitted, I do not see how the RPD allegedly erred with respect to this finding. There was indeed no evidence submitted that demonstrates the minor appellants' well-founded fear of persecution or a fear of being subjected to a risk to their lives under section 97 of the IRPA, if they had to return to their country of citizenship.
Consequently, in light of the above, I find that the appellants failed to demonstrate that the RPD committed errors justifying the RAD's intervention.

For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA or "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed. Normand Leduc Normand Leduc July 6, 2018 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 RAD.25.02 (April 9, 2013) Disponible en français RAD File No. / N° de dossier de la SAR : MB7-22430; MB7-22431; MB7-22432 7
